notes: Peter is called by Jesus and named chief of the Twelve in all four Gospels.
One of the Twelve who later betrayed Jesus.
Acts 1:21-22 specifies Matthias had accompanied Jesus 'beginning from the baptism of John' though he was not one of the original Twelve.
Brother of Jesus per Mark 6:3 and Galatians 1:19; received a resurrection appearance per 1 Cor 15:7.
Paul claims a resurrection appearance and direct revelation (Galatians 1:11-17, 1 Cor 15:8). Not a pre-Easter disciple.
Paul visited Cephas in Jerusalem for fifteen days c. AD 36 (Gal 1:18). They later met at the Apostolic Council (Gal 2 / Acts 15).
The Antioch incident: Paul publicly rebuked Peter for withdrawing from Gentile table fellowship under pressure from 'men from James' (Gal 2:11-14).
Paul met James in Jerusalem (Gal 1:19) and again at the Apostolic Council (Gal 2:9 / Acts 15).

Paul was opposed not by James personally but by 'certain men from James' whose intervention triggered the Antioch incident (Gal 2:12). The direct opposition between Paul and James himself is inferred and disputed by scholars.

Mark accompanied Paul and Barnabas, then split (Acts 13:13; 15:37-39). Later reconciled (Col 4:10; 2 Tim 4:11).

Papias (c. 110-130) reports Mark was Peter's interpreter and recorded Peter's preaching as the Gospel of Mark — but Papias' testimony itself survives only via Eusebius. 1 Peter 5:13 mentions 'Mark my son' but does not establish discipleship.

Irenaeus, who personally heard Polycarp in his youth, states in Adv. Haer. 3.3.4 and his Letter to Florinus (Eus. HE 5.20) that Polycarp was instructed by John and 'others who had seen the Lord'. This is a near-contemporary chain (Irenaeus -> Polycarp -> John), so 'documented'.

citations.source: Irenaeus, Letter to Florinus, in Eusebius HE 5.20.4-8

notes: Later tradition (e.g. the Martyrium Ignatii and John Chrysostom) makes Ignatius a disciple of John alongside Polycarp; not attested by Ignatius himself or by Irenaeus.

Irenaeus calls Papias 'a hearer of John' (Adv. Haer. 5.33.4), but Eusebius (HE 3.39.5-7), reading Papias' own preface, argues Papias heard 'the elder John', a different figure. Borderline — flagged for review.
Whether or not Papias heard John the Apostle directly, his preface explicitly reports gathering sayings of John (the Lord's disciple) via the elders.
Forward edge into the next era. Irenaeus in his Letter to Florinus describes hearing Polycarp preach in his youth at Smyrna.

citations.source: Irenaeus, Letter to Florinus in Eusebius HE 5.20.4-8

Roman succession list reconstructed by Irenaeus c. 180; no contemporaneous attestation.
Roman succession list reconstructed by Irenaeus c. 180; the order Linus-Anacletus-Clement is not contemporaneously attested.

Irenaeus (Adv. Haer. 5.33.4) calls Papias 'a companion of Polycarp'. No surviving first-person source.
Strictly an apostolic succession (not episcopal) — Matthias chosen by lot to replace Judas among the Twelve.
Roman Catholic tradition treats Peter as Christ's vicar / successor in pastoral leadership of the Church (Matt 16:18-19); not framed as episcopal succession in the New Testament itself.
Papias preserves the earliest tradition about Mark's authorship and method.
Quadratus' surviving fragment claims firsthand testimony was still alive in his day from those healed or raised by Jesus.

notes: The Shepherd (Vis. 2.4.3) instructs Hermas to give a copy of the book to 'Clement', who will send it abroad. The identification with Clement of Rome is plausible but traditional, and the Muratorian Fragment dates Hermas under Pius I (mid-2nd c.) which would post-date Clement.
Polycarp's Letter to the Philippians quotes or alludes to most of the Pauline corpus extensively.
Ignatius alludes repeatedly to Pauline letters (esp. 1 Cor, Eph) and explicitly praises Paul (Eph. 12.2; Rom. 4.3).
The Didache cites the Lord's Prayer and dominical sayings 'as the Lord commanded in his Gospel'.
Mary is the mother of Jesus per the infancy narratives of Matthew and Luke; present at the wedding at Cana, the crucifixion, and with the disciples before Pentecost.
From the cross Jesus entrusted his mother to the Beloved Disciple, who took her into his own home (John 19:26-27).

Clement of Alexandria quotes the Epistle of Barnabas as scripture in the Stromata, attributing it to the apostolic Barnabas. Marked tradition because Pseudo-Barnabas himself is anonymous; Clement is citing the text under a pseudepigraphic attribution.
Origen quotes the Epistle of Barnabas as a 'catholic epistle' (Contra Celsum 1.63). Marked tradition because Pseudo-Barnabas is anonymous and Origen attributes the text to the apostolic Barnabas.
Eusebius discusses the Epistle of Barnabas among the disputed/spurious writings (HE 3.25, 6.14). Marked tradition because the author is anonymous.
Irenaeus describes in his Letter to Florinus hearing Polycarp preach in his youth in Smyrna and remembering his testimony about John the Apostle. This is direct first-person testimony.

citations.source: Irenaeus, Letter to Florinus (in Eusebius HE 5.20)

notes: Tatian was a disciple of Justin in Rome and only fell into heterodoxy after Justin's martyrdom.
Clement names Pantaenus as the 'true Sicilian bee' from whom he received instruction.
Clement succeeded Pantaenus as head of the Catechetical School of Alexandria. Eusebius (HE 6.6) is the source; Clement's own writings name Pantaenus as teacher but not as predecessor in office.
Eusebius implies Origen heard Clement at the Catechetical School; some scholars treat this as inferred rather than firmly attested.
Origen succeeded Clement as head of the Catechetical School c. 203 after Clement fled persecution. Source is Eusebius HE 6.3, 6.6; Origen himself does not narrate the succession.
Gregory studied under Origen at Caesarea for several years and wrote a famous panegyric upon leaving.
Dionysius was a pupil of Origen at Alexandria and later headed the Catechetical School.
Heraclas studied alongside, then under, Origen and shared in teaching the catechumens.
Heraclas succeeded Origen as head of the Catechetical School after Origen's departure to Caesarea.
Dionysius succeeded Heraclas as bishop of Alexandria in 247.
Demetrius initially appointed Origen but later condemned him in synods after his ordination at Caesarea, expelling him from Alexandria.
Heraclas became 13th bishop of Alexandria in 231 succeeding Demetrius.
Jerome (late 4th c., De Vir. Ill. 53) reports that Cyprian read Tertullian daily, asking 'Da magistrum'. Cyprian himself never names Tertullian; the link is Jerome's anecdote 130+ years later.
Jerome (De Vir. Ill. 80, c. 393) states Lactantius was a pupil of Arnobius at Sicca; no contemporary attestation, and Lactantius himself does not name Arnobius.
The bulk of Adversus Haereses is directed against the Valentinian system.
Irenaeus refutes Marcion's truncated canon and dualism.
Irenaeus refutes the system of Basilides.
Tertullian's five books Adversus Marcionem are the most extensive ancient refutation.
Tertullian's Adversus Valentinianos refutes the Valentinian school.
Hippolytus' Refutatio devotes considerable space to refuting Valentinian and other Gnostic systems.
Hippolytus gives an extended refutation of Basilides in Refutatio book 7.
Photius and later sources describe Hippolytus as a hearer of Irenaeus; some modern scholars treat the link as plausible but not directly attested.
Hippolytus accuses Zephyrinus of doctrinal weakness and Callixtus of innovation in penance.
Hippolytus rejected Callixtus' election and his lenient discipline; tradition makes him an antipope of this period.
Tertullian's De Pudicitia attacks the unnamed bishop (commonly identified as Callixtus) for absolving adultery.
Polycarp visited Anicetus in Rome; they discussed the Quartodeciman question and parted in peace.

Dionysius wrote to Stephen urging moderation in the rebaptism dispute.

Lifelong friendship from Thagaste through Carthage, Rome, Milan and back to Africa.

Augustine was deeply moved by hearing of the conversion of Marius Victorinus.
Extensive (often acrimonious) correspondence over Galatians and the Hebrew text of the OT.
Friends from youth in Aquileia who became bitter opponents over Origenism.
The Origenist controversy split the two former friends c. 393-402.
Damasus commissioned Jerome's revision of the Latin Bible.
Jerome and Epiphanius were close allies in the Origenist controversy.

Rufinus translated and continued Eusebius's HE.
The Pelagian controversy occupied Augustine's last two decades.
Augustine wrote six books Contra Julianum and the unfinished Opus Imperfectum.
Augustine wrote against Caelestius alongside Pelagius.

Innocent became Bishop of Rome (401) following Anastasius, Siricius, and Damasus — three intervening bishops. Source is the Liber Pontificalis.
Chrysostom appealed to Innocent after his deposition.

Flavian became Archbishop of Constantinople (446) several bishops after Nestorius (Maximian, Proclus); not a direct succession.
Cyril became Patriarch of Alexandria (412) several bishops after Athanasius (d. 373) — Peter II, Timothy, Theophilus all intervened. Not a direct succession.
Marcellus and Athanasius were exiled to Rome together c. 339-343.

notes: Gregory uses Sulpicius's Vita Martini extensively as the source for his own four books of miracles of Saint Martin and cites it explicitly.

citations.source: Gregory of Tours, Libri de virtutibus sancti Martini, prologue and 1.2

notes: Gregory cites Augustine's De civitate Dei and Augustine's exegesis at several points in his Histories and miracle books.

citations.source: Gregory of Tours, Hist. Franc. 1 prologue

notes: Heraclius promoted Monoenergism/Monothelitism via the Ekthesis (638) and Patriarch Sergius's Psephos; Sophronius led ecclesial opposition culminating in his synodical letter of 634.

citations.source: Sophronius, Synodical Letter (634), in ACO ser. II vol. 2

notes: Agatho's dogmatic letter (Tomus Agathonis) read at the Third Council of Constantinople (681) explicitly invokes and incorporates the Tome of Leo as the standard of Chalcedonian dyothelite Christology.

notes: The Ladder of Divine Ascent depends pervasively on Evagrian ascetic psychology (the eight logismoi, apatheia) though it carefully avoids Evagrius's name; the dependence is uncontroversial in scholarship.

citations.source: John Climacus, Ladder of Divine Ascent, steps 13-15, 26
Chryssavgis, John Climacus: From the Egyptian Desert to the Sinaite Mountain (Ashgate 2004), ch. 4

notes: Maximus (d. 662) draws on Sinaitic ascetic literature; Climacus (d. c. 649) is older. Direct quotation is not formal but Maximus's spiritual anthropology shares Climacus's framework.
Palladius reports Macarius of Alexandria as a disciple of Antony; the relationship is preserved in the desert-father tradition rather than in a contemporary document.
Palladius records Melania the Elder visiting Pambo at Nitria shortly before his death and Pambo dying in her presence.
Sisoes settled on Antony's mountain (Mount Colzim) after Antony's death; this is a hagiographic succession of place rather than an episcopal see, but is the standard tradition. Use with caution.

citations.source: Apophthegmata Patrum, alphabetical collection s.v. Sisoes 1, 28

notes: Besa's Vita Sinuthii reports Shenoute accompanying Cyril to the Council of Ephesus in 431; this is attested in the hagiographic tradition rather than in conciliar acta.

Aphrahat (writing 337-345 in Sasanian Persia) and Ephrem (in Roman Nisibis/Edessa) are the two great early Syriac authors and near-contemporaries. Direct contact is not attested in primary sources; the linkage is a scholarly/traditional pairing of the founders of Syriac theological literature.

citations.source: Sebastian Brock, A Brief Outline of Syriac Literature

notes: Severus rejected the Tome of Leo and the Christological definition of Chalcedon (451), polemicising against Leo's two-natures formula across his letters and treatises (e.g. Contra impium Grammaticum, Philalethes).

citations.source: Severus of Antioch, Liber contra impium Grammaticum

notes: A small corpus of letters attributed to Jacob includes correspondence with Severus's miaphysite circle; the authenticity of individual letters is debated but the broader correspondence is generally accepted.
Gregory's two letters to Cledonius (Ep. 101, 102) are the classic Cappadocian refutation of Apollinarian Christology, with the famous formula 'what has not been assumed has not been healed.'
Gregory of Nyssa wrote the Antirrheticus adversus Apollinarem, a sustained refutation of Apollinaris's treatise on the Incarnation.

citations.source: Gregory of Nyssa, Antirrheticus adversus Apollinarem

notes: Epiphanius devotes Panarion 77 to refuting the Apollinarians.
Theodoret treats Apollinarianism in his heresiological compendium and elsewhere as a Christological error denying Christ's full humanity.
Augustine preached three surviving sermons (280-282) on the feast of Perpetua and Felicity at Carthage and Hippo.
Augustine's sermons 280-282 commemorate Felicity jointly with Perpetua.
Paula and Eustochium are joint addressees of numerous Hieronymian letters and prefaces; Jerome composed her epitaph.
Jerome's epitaph for Paula recounts her hosting Epiphanius in Rome and visiting him at Salamis on her journey east.
Daughter of Paula; raised in her mother's ascetic household and succeeded her as head of the Bethlehem women's monastery.
Recipient of Jerome's Letter 22 (Ad Eustochium) and dedicatee of multiple biblical commentaries.

citations.source: Jerome, prefaces to commentaries on Isaiah, Ezekiel and the Minor Prophets

notes: Palladius records Melania the Elder as a patron and correspondent of Evagrius at Kellia.
Co-founders of the double monastery on the Mount of Olives c. 374-378.
Gerontius's Vita records Melania and Pinianus residing near Hippo c. 410-417 and meeting Augustine and Alypius; Augustine's Letter 124 is addressed to them.
Vita Melaniae reports a visit to Alexandria where she received Cyril; primary attestation rests on the Vita alone.
Granddaughter; the Vita stresses Melania the Elder's ascetic example as decisive for the younger Melania's vocation.
Seventeen letters from Chrysostom to Olympias survive, written largely from his exile.

citations.source: Palladius, Dialogus de Vita Iohannis Chrysostomi 16-17
